title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?

paper.title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
paper.abstract:
Abstract The escape fraction of ionizing photons, f esc f_{\rm esc} , is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) , and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) , against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow f esc f_{\rm esc} to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant- f esc f_{\rm esc} model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from ≈ 0.8 \approx 0.8 at z = 5 z=5 to ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 at z = 15 z=15 . The halo-mass-only model prefers f esc f_{\rm esc} increasing with halo mass, but this
trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent f esc f_{\rm esc} . At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within ≈ 10 % \approx 10\% . These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the f esc f_{\rm esc} prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Ly α \alpha and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) marks the last major phase transition of the universe from a neutral to an ionized state [ 106 , 21 , for recent reviews, see] . The first stars and galaxies, which formed during the Cosmic Dawn, produced copious Lyman continuum (LyC) photons that ionized the neutral hydrogen in the surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM), forming ionized bubbles around them [ 4 , 112 , 26 ] . Over time, these bubbles grew and eventually overlapped, marking the completion of reionization. However, most of these ionizing photons could not escape their host galaxies and were instead absorbed by neutral gas and dust in the interstellar medium and circumgalactic medium [ 101 ] . The fraction that does escape into the IGM is referred to as the ionizing photon escape fraction ( f esc f_{\rm esc} ) [ 98 , 108 ] . Understanding f esc f_{\rm esc} is critical for establishing both the physical mechanisms and the timeline of reionization. Together with the ionizing photon production efficiency ( ξ ion \xi_{\rm ion} ) and the star formation history, it sets the ionizing emissivity, and therefore governs whether reionization proceeded rapidly or gradually and which sources drove it. Pre-JWST models combined with Planck observations suggest that star-forming galaxies produce enough ionizing photons to reionize the universe by z ∼ 6 z\sim 6 . S. L. Finkelstein et al. [35] , for example, argued that a low, halo-mass-dependent escape fraction with a global average of only a few percent ( ⟨ f esc ⟩ ≤ 5 % \langle f_{\rm esc}\rangle\leq 5\% ) is sufficient to complete reionization. That conclusion relies on several key assumptions, including star formation extending down to ultra-faint galaxies (a faint-end truncation at M UV ∼ − 13 M_{\rm UV}\sim-13 with photo-suppression quenching star formation below log ⁡ ( M h / M ⊙ ) ∼ 9 \log(M_{\rm h}/M_{\odot})\sim 9 in already-ionized regions), an ionizing photon production efficiency that rises modestly toward fainter, higher-redshift dwarfs ( log ⁡ ξ ion ∼ 25.2 \log\xi_{\rm ion}\sim 25.2 – 25.3 25.3 ), and a significant but subdominant active galactic nucleus (AGN) contribution at z ≲ 7 z\lesssim 7 . However, the JWST observations have revealed an overabundance of UV-luminous galaxies at z ≳ 9 z\gtrsim 9 [ 19 , 48 , 36 ] together with elevated ionizing efficiencies ( log ⁡ ξ ion ≈ 25.5 \log\xi_{\rm ion}\approx 25.5 – 26.0 26.0 ) [ 32 , 82 ] , which imply far more ionizing photons at early times. Taken at face value, these photons would complete reionization too early, in tension with the low CMB Thomson optical depth measured by Planck Collaboration et al. [90] and with Lyman- α \alpha forest measurements, which place the end of reionization near z ∼ 5.5 z\sim 5.5 [ 7 , 13 ] , later than the z ∼ 6 z\sim 6 endpoint assumed in earlier models, termed as “photon budget crisis” [ 82 ] . Several resolutions have been proposed, including bursty star formation inflating the observed UV luminosity function [ 99 ] , a shorter ionizing mean free path [ 8 ] , a truncation of the faint-end galaxy population [ 82 ] , and a revised ξ ion \xi_{\rm ion} [ 96 ] . The possibility we examine here is that the escape fraction of these abundant early galaxies is lower, and/or suppressed toward higher redshift, than low-redshift LyC leaker calibrations imply [ 39 ] . The IGM is opaque to the ionizing photons at high redshifts, so f esc f_{\rm esc} cannot be measured directly during this era [ 59 ] . We therefore rely on models that predict its behavior by constraining it against other available observables [ 92 , 81 , e.g.,] . Physically, f esc f_{\rm esc} is set by the interstellar medium (ISM) on scales far below those resolved in reionization simulations. Young stars emit most of their ionizing photons within the first few Myr, while still embedded in dense birth clouds that absorb them [ 62 , 69 ] . Photons escape mainly through low-column-density channels cleared by stellar and supernova feedback, so f esc f_{\rm esc} peaks only after a delay and varies strongly with the recent star formation history [ 62 , 69 ] . Processes that extend the ionizing output beyond this delay, such as binary stellar evolution [ 68 ] and runaway massive stars [ 62 ] , increase the escape fraction, although in the FIRE-2 simulations binaries raise ⟨ f esc ⟩ \langle f_{\rm esc}\rangle by only ≈ 25 \approx 25 –35% [ 70 ] . C. Howard et al. [56] suggest that the escape fraction is a strongly fluctuating quantity that depends on the mass of the star cluster and the turbulent structure of the gas cloud. M. Trebitsch et al. [101] , using a series of high-resolution radiation hydrodynamical simulations, find that f esc f_{\rm esc} in high-redshift galaxies can vary by several orders of magnitude over short timescales, driven primarily by supernova explosions that disrupt dense star-forming clumps and clear low-column-density channels through the halo. Averaged over a galaxy population, the escape fraction depends on the physical properties of the host galaxies [ 62 ] , which correlate with halo mass ( M h M_{\rm h} ) [ 109 ] . Simulations of the first galaxies find that feedback clears escape channels more easily in low-mass halos, giving an escape fraction that decreases with halo mass [ 107 , 86 , 109 , 63 ] , a trend adopted in several reionization models [ 87 , 35 ] . Because low-mass halos dominate at early times, such models imply a population-averaged escape fraction that increases with redshift, as also assumed in earlier emissivity models [ 47 , 65 ] . However, simulations disagree on the strength and even the sign of the resulting f esc f_{\rm esc} – M h M_{\rm h} trend [ 70 ] . We therefore treat any f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) relation as a population-averaged parametrization rather than a description of individual galaxies. While many models adopt a constant f esc f_{\rm esc} for convenience, this fails to capture the dynamics of galaxy evolution. For example, S. Mitra & A. Chatterjee [80] use a data-driven reionization model with a Gaussian Process Regression method to infer a redshift-dependent escape fraction, though that reconstruction relies on pre-JWST data. To capture the dynamics of the escape fraction, in this paper we consider three simple prescriptions of photon escape fraction that depend on redshift, halo mass, and the both: f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) , and compare with a constant f esc f_{\rm esc} baseline model of A. Bera et al. [10] . We constrain these models against JWST and EoR observables, namely the UV luminosity functions, the IGM neutral fraction, and the CMB optical depth, using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework to obtain posterior constraints on the model parameters and to trace the evolution of the escape fraction with redshift and/or halo mass. We then integrate our MCMC-calibrated f esc f_{\rm esc} prescriptions directly into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 [ 93 ] . While full radiative transfer codes such as C 2 -Ray [ 77 ] are more physically robust, they are computationally expensive. Other semi-numerical alternatives include excursion-set frameworks [ 79 , e.g., 21cmFAST ;] , one-dimensional radiative transfer schemes [ 44 , GRIZZLY ;] , explicitly photon-conserving algorithms [ 22 , 23 , SCRIPT ;] , abundance-matching approaches [ 100 , AMBER ;] , and models coupled to semi-analytic galaxy formation [ 58 , ASTRAEUS ;] . SimFast21 is based on the excursion-set formalism but populates the non-linear density field with resolved halos. This allows us to move beyond globally averaged reionization histories to the full three-dimensional ionization field, quantifying whether, and to what extent, an evolving escape fraction alters the morphology of ionized bubbles and the resulting 21-cm power spectra at fixed neutral fraction. This paper is organized as follows. In Section II , we describe the source model, combining the intrinsic ionizing photon production rate with our three f esc f_{\rm esc} parameterizations. Section III describes how the UV luminosity function, ionizing emissivity, neutral hydrogen fraction, and Thomson optical depth are computed in the model, and lists the observational data used to constrain them. In Section IV , we present the MCMC framework and our implementation of the f esc f_{\rm esc} models in SimFast21 . Section V presents the MCMC constraints on the escape fraction, followed by the ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra from the simulations. We summarize our conclusions and discuss future directions in Section VI .

sections.heading: II Source model
sections.text: In this section we describe the source model that governs the ionizing photon budget, combining a prescription for the intrinsic photon production rate with the redshift- and halo-mass-dependent escape-fraction models.

sections.heading: II.1 Ionization Rate, R ion R_{\rm ion}
sections.text: To quantify the intrinsic production rate of ionizing photons, we adopt the source model of S. Hassan et al. [51] , with the ionization rate, R ion R_{\rm ion} (in units of photons s -1 ) as a function of halo mass ( M h M_{\rm h} ) and redshift ( z z ), derived from radiative-transfer simulations [ 38 ] . This model has previously been calibrated against EoR observables [ 11 ] and JWST constraints [ 10 ] . The ionization rate is given by R ion = A × M h ​ ( 1 + z ) D ​ ( M h B ) C ​ exp ⁡ [ − ( M h B ) − 3 ] R_{\rm ion}=A\times M_{\rm h}\left(1+z\right)^{D}\left(\frac{M_{\rm h}}{B}\right)^{C}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{M_{\rm h}}{B}\right)^{-3}\right] (1) The mass dependence in this relation is Schechter-like, a power law at the massive end and an exponential turnover at low masses due to supernova and photoionization feedback, while the redshift dependence is a simple power law. Here A A , B B , C C and D D are free parameters. The parameter A A acts as the overall amplitude factor with units of s M − 1 ⊙ − 1 {}^{-1}\,M_{\odot}^{-1} . B B is the characteristic quenching mass scale below which photon production is exponentially suppressed by feedback, with units of M ⊙ M_{\odot} . The parameter C C sets the slope of the R ion − M h R_{\rm ion}-M_{\rm h} relation, so larger C C shifts the ionizing budget toward massive halos. D D accounts for the redshift dependence in the ionizing photon production rate. The rate of ionizing photons that escape a halo is obtained by multiplying R ion R_{\rm ion} with the escape fraction f esc f_{\rm esc} .

sections.heading: II.2 The ionizing photon escape fraction
sections.text: The physical dependences of the population-averaged escape fraction remain uncertain, and previous studies have parameterized it as a function of either halo mass or redshift. We consider power-law parameterizations in both, following J. Park et al. [87] , who model f esc f_{\rm esc} as a power law in halo mass, and C.-A. Faucher-Giguère [34] , who model it as f esc ∝ ( 1 + z ) γ f_{\rm esc}\propto(1+z)^{\gamma} . We define three functional forms: f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) , and a combined f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) . A redshift-dependent escape fraction has been inferred from data-driven reionization models [ 80 ] and adopted in models of the UV background [ 47 , 34 ] . Post-processing of TNG50 likewise finds that the average escape fraction of low-mass galaxies evolves with redshift [ 64 ] . In our first model, f esc f_{\rm esc} depends only on redshift: f esc ​ ( z ) = a ​ ( 1 + z 6 ) b z , f_{\rm esc}(z)=a\left(\frac{1+z}{6}\right)^{b_{\rm z}}, (2) where a a is the escape fraction at z = 5 z=5 and b z b_{\rm z} is the redshift power-law index. A dependence on halo mass is expected because the gas column density around young stars and the efficiency with which feedback clears escape channels both vary with the host. Simulations of the first galaxies find an escape fraction that decreases with halo mass [ 107 , 86 , 109 ] , while others find a weak [ 62 ] or non-monotonic [ 70 ] dependence. sections.heading: III Observational Constraints
sections.text: To constrain the free parameters of our f esc f_{\rm esc} models, we compare the model predictions against JWST and EoR observables. All data are compiled using the publicly available CoReCon package [ 43 ] , following the compilation of A. Bera et al. [10] . In the following subsections, we describe how each observable is computed in the model and list the datasets used in the likelihood (Section IV.1 ).

sections.heading: IV Computational Methodology
sections.text: To connect our f esc f_{\rm esc} parametrizations to observables, we constrain the model parameters with an MCMC framework and propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical code SimFast21 to predict the three-dimensional ionization and 21-cm fields.

sections.heading: IV.1 MCMC Implementation
sections.text: We fit each f esc f_{\rm esc} model to the EoR and JWST observables (Section III ) and sample the posterior with the affine-invariant ensemble sampler emcee [ 40 ] . We adopt flat priors on a ∈ [ 0.01 , 1 ] a\in[0.01,1] , b z ∈ [ − 5 , 5 ] b_{z}\in[-5,5] , b m ∈ [ − 5 , 5 ] b_{m}\in[-5,5] , log 10 ⁡ A ∈ [ 35 , 45 ] \log_{10}A\in[35,45] , C ∈ [ − 10 , 10 ] C\in[-10,10] , and D ∈ [ − 5 , 10 ] D\in[-5,10] . The priors on b z b_{z} and b m b_{m} are symmetric about zero and admit both signs of each dependence, including escape fractions that increase with redshift or decrease with halo mass, as proposed for feedback-regulated low-mass galaxies (Section I ). Following A. Bera et al. [11] , we fix log 10 ⁡ ( B / M ⊙ ) = 7.67 \log_{10}(B/M_{\odot})=7.67 . The sampled parameter vectors are θ = { a , b z , A , C , D } \theta=\{a,b_{z},A,C,D\} for f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , θ = { a , b m , A , C , D } \theta=\{a,b_{m},A,C,D\} for f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) , and θ = { a , b z , b m , A , C , D } \theta=\{a,b_{z},b_{m},A,C,D\} for f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) . To keep f esc f_{\rm esc} physical, we assign zero prior probability to any parameter combination that yields f esc > 1 f_{\rm esc}>1 within the redshift and halo-mass range of the model. We compute the log-likelihood for each observable separately and treat them as independent, and hence the total log-likelihood is ln ⁡ ℒ tot ​ ( θ ) = ln ⁡ ℒ x HI + ln ⁡ ℒ τ + ln ⁡ ℒ n ˙ ion + ln ⁡ ℒ UVLF . \ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm tot}({\theta})=\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm x_{\rm HI}}+\ln\mathcal{L}_{\tau}+\ln\mathcal{L}_{\dot{n}_{\rm ion}}+\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm UVLF}\,. (16) Each observable is modeled as a Gaussian likelihood. For example, the log-likelihood for the neutral hydrogen fraction is ln ⁡ ℒ x HI ​ ( θ ) = − 1 2 ​ ( x HI , obs − x HI , model σ x HI ) 2 {\rm\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm x_{\rm HI}}(\rm\theta)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\rm x_{\rm HI,obs}-x_{\rm HI,model}}{\rm\sigma_{\rm x_{\rm HI}}}\right)^{2}} (17) The MCMC framework yields globally averaged quantities, which carry no information about the spatial distribution of ionized and neutral gas. Many distinct distributions can yield the same global averages: for instance, a reionization history driven by many small ionized bubbles can reproduce the same volume-averaged ionized fraction as one driven by a few large bubbles. To test whether f esc f_{\rm esc} models calibrated to the same global observables produce distinguishable ionization morphologies and 21-cm power spectra, we use SimFast21 (Section IV.2 ).

sections.heading: IV.2 SimFast21
sections.text: We use the best-fit parameters from the MCMC to generate ionization and 21-cm differential brightness temperature fields with the semi-numerical code SimFast21 [ 93 , 53 , 51 ] . SimFast21 generates a linear Gaussian random density field, evolves it into the non-linear regime using the Y. B. Zel’dovich [113] approximation, and identifies collapsed halos with an excursion-set halo finder applied to the evolved field. The non-linear density field sets both the halo distribution and the density of the surrounding IGM. These are used to compute the ionization rate, which depends on halo mass, and the recombination rate that depends on the local overdensity, and finally the 21-cm brightness temperature field. The source model follows S. Hassan et al. [51] , who calibrated R ion R_{\rm ion} as a function of halo mass and redshift by combining the high-resolution radiative hydrodynamic simulation of K. Finlator et al. [38, 6/256-RT] with the larger-volume hydrodynamic simulation of R. Davé et al. [25] , and the functional form is given in Eq. 1 . sections.heading: V Results
sections.text: In this section we first present the MCMC constraints on the three variable f esc f_{\rm esc} models (Section V.1 ), and then use the best-fit parameters to drive our SimFast21 simulations (Section V.2 ). Throughout, we compare our results against the constant f esc f_{\rm esc} model of A. Bera et al. [10] . The models are color-coded consistently in all figures: f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) in blue, f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) in green, f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) in red, and constant f esc f_{\rm esc} in black, unless otherwise specified.

For the escape-fraction parameters, the amplitude a a is anticorrelated with the power-law index in all three models: lower values of a a are compensated by a higher b z b_{z} or b m b_{m} . This degeneracy direction indicates that the data constrain f esc f_{\rm esc} most tightly at z > 5 z>5 and M h > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\rm h}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} rather than at the reference values. In the redshift-dependent models, a a lies close to the upper bound imposed by the physical prior f esc ≤ 1 f_{\rm esc}\leq 1 . In the combined model, b z b_{z} is constrained away from zero while b m b_{m} is consistent with zero. A negative b z b_{z} and a positive b m b_{m} both make the average f esc f_{\rm esc} decline toward higher redshift, the latter because low-mass halos dominate the halo population at early times. The two indices are therefore positively correlated in the combined model (Figure 1 ): a less negative b z b_{z} can be partly compensated by a positive b m b_{m} . This produces the tails in the a a and b z b_{z} posteriors toward lower a a and less negative b z b_{z} , which otherwise peak close to those of the f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) model. [35] , in which faint galaxies dominate the ionizing emissivity and the globally averaged escape fraction increases toward higher redshift, reaching f esc ≈ 0.14 f_{\rm esc}\approx 0.14 at z ∼ 15 z\sim 15 . [107] find that the luminosity-weighted f esc f_{\rm esc} decreases from ≈ 0.5 \approx 0.5 in halos of 10 6.5 10^{6.5} – 10 7 ​ M ⊙ 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} to ≈ 0.25 \approx 0.25 at 10 8 ​ M ⊙ 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} and ≈ 0.05 \approx 0.05 at 10 8.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{8.5}\,M_{\odot} , and J.-P. [70] , spanning M vir ∼ 10 8 M_{\rm vir}\sim 10^{8} – 10 12 ​ M ⊙ 10^{12}\,M_{\odot} at z = 5 z=5 –12, give a non-monotonic trend: ⟨ f esc ⟩ \langle f_{\rm esc}\rangle increases with halo mass up to ∼ 10 9.5 ​ M ⊙ \sim 10^{9.5}\,M_{\odot} , is nearly constant ( ≈ 0.1 \approx 0.1 –0.2, depending on resolution) up to ∼ 10 11 ​ M ⊙ \sim 10^{11}\,M_{\odot} , and declines at higher masses owing to dust attenuation. sections.heading: V.2.1 Morphology of the ionization field
sections.text: Since the three f esc f_{\rm esc} parameterizations produce nearly identical histories of N ˙ ion \dot{N}_{\rm ion} , x HI x_{\rm HI} , and τ \tau , the question is whether they remain degenerate at the level of the spatial structure of reionization, which the volume-averaged quantities do not probe. Figure 7 shows slices of the ionized fraction x HII x_{\rm HII} through the simulation volume for the constant f esc f_{\rm esc} model and for each of our three dynamical f esc f_{\rm esc} parameterizations. All four runs share the same initial conditions, so the underlying density field and the locations of ionizing sources are identical by construction, any difference between the panels is therefore attributable to the escape-fraction prescription alone. The panels in figure 7 are selected at approximately matched global neutral fractions, ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.95 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.95 , 0.5 0.5 , and 0.25 0.25 , rather than at fixed redshift. Comparing at fixed ⟨ x HI ⟩ \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle isolates differences in the morphology of reionization from differences in its timing. The redshifts at which each model reaches a given stage are quoted above each panel. At all three stages the ionization morphology is closely similar across the four models. The earliest snapshots show small, isolated ionized regions tracing the most massive halos, embedded in an otherwise neutral IGM. By the midpoint of reionization the individual bubbles have grown and begun to overlap into extended ionized regions that follow the filamentary structure of the density field, and by ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.25 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.25 the ionized regions overlap, leaving the remaining neutral gas confined to under-dense regions between them. This is the standard inside-out topology expected for galaxy-driven reionization, and it is reproduced by every escape-fraction prescription we consider. In particular, the f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) slices are visually indistinguishable from one another at all three stages, as expected given that the combined model has a halo-mass index consistent with zero (Section V.1 ). The models differ only in the redshift at which a given stage is reached, and these differences are small. The mass-dependent model is the most advanced at fixed redshift, reaching ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.5 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.5 at z = 7.8 z=7.8 and ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.24 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.24 at z = 6.6 z=6.6 , while the constant f esc f_{\rm esc} model reaches the same stages at z = 7.6 z=7.6 and z = 6.4 z=6.4 respectively. The two redshift-dependent models begin slightly later than the others, reaching ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.95 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.95 at z = 13.0 z=13.0 rather than z = 13.4 z=13.4 , consistent with their negative redshift index suppressing f esc f_{\rm esc} at early times. All of these offsets are Δ ​ z ≲ 0.4 \Delta z\lesssim 0.4 , comparable to a small multiple of the output spacing Δ ​ z = 0.2 \Delta z=0.2 , and the corresponding continuous ionization histories agree to well within the observational uncertainties (Figure 5 ).

sections.heading: V.2.2 The 21 cm power spectrum
sections.text: The ionization slices of Figure 7 suggest that the four escape-fraction prescriptions produce similar spatial structure. We therefore compute the spherically averaged dimensionless power spectrum of the 21 cm brightness temperature, Δ 2 ​ ( k ) = k 3 2 ​ π 2 ​ P δ ​ T b ​ ( k ) , \Delta^{2}(k)=\frac{k^{3}}{2\pi^{2}}\,P_{\delta T_{\rm b}}(k), (19) for each model at the same three stages of reionization used in Figure 7 . As with the slices, the comparison is made at matched global neutral fraction rather than at fixed redshift. This distinction is essential. Evaluated at a common redshift the models differ in Δ 2 ​ ( k ) \Delta^{2}(k) by a factor of several, but this reflects the fact that they reach a given stage of reionization at slightly different times: the mean brightness temperature scales as ⟨ δ ​ T b ⟩ ∝ ⟨ x HI ⟩ \langle\delta T_{\rm b}\rangle\propto\langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle to leading order, so the power scales as its square, and a modest offset in ionization history produces a large offset in amplitude. Matching in ⟨ x HI ⟩ \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle removes this timing effect and isolates differences in the spatial distribution of the neutral gas. We quantify these differences in Table 3 , which lists, for each model and stage, the median and maximum fractional deviation of Δ 2 ​ ( k ) \Delta^{2}(k) from the constant- f esc f_{\rm esc} model, | Δ model 2 ​ ( k ) / Δ const 2 ​ ( k ) − 1 | |\Delta^{2}_{\rm model}(k)/\Delta^{2}_{\rm const}(k)-1| , over k > 0.2 ​ h ​ Mpc − 1 k>0.2\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1} . The ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.95 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.95 stage serves as a test: the ionization field is negligible at this point, so any deviation reflects the snapshot selection rather than differences in ionization morphology. Figure 8 and Table 3 show that at the earliest stage, ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.95 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.95 , the models agree to within 6 % 6\% for k > 0.2 ​ h ​ Mpc − 1 k>0.2\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1} , with a median deviation of 3 % 3\% from the constant f esc f_{\rm esc} case. The two redshift-dependent models, f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) , track one another closely, consistent with the near-zero halo-mass index recovered for the combined model (Section V.1 ) and with their indistinguishable ionization slices. These are also the two models that reach ⟨ x HI ⟩ ≃ 0.95 \langle x_{\rm HI}\rangle\simeq 0.95 at z = 13.0 z=13.0 rather than z = 13.4 z=13.4 . sections.heading: VI Conclusions & Discussion
sections.text: JWST observations have revealed an abundance of UV-luminous galaxies at z ≳ 9 z\gtrsim 9 which, combined with the source models of the pre-JWST era, would overproduce ionizing photons and complete reionization too early. In this work we tested whether a variable ionizing photon escape fraction can accommodate these observations. We parameterized f esc f_{\rm esc} as a function of redshift, halo mass, and both, with priors that allow either sign of each dependence, constrained each parameterization against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables ( x HI x_{\rm HI} , N ˙ ion \dot{N}_{\rm ion} , τ \tau ) with an MCMC framework, and propagated the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 to compare the resulting ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant- f esc f_{\rm esc} reference model. Our main findings are as follows. 1. The data require an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from ≈ 0.8 \approx 0.8 at z = 5 z=5 to ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 at z = 15 z=15 . This behavior is common to all three variable models; in the f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) model it emerges through the evolving halo population rather than through an explicit redshift term. Although the priors admit both signs, an escape fraction that increases with redshift, as adopted in earlier reionization models [ 47 , 65 , 35 ] , is excluded (see Figure 2 and Table 2 ). Because the UVLF fixes the intrinsic ionizing photon production while the EoR observables constrain the escaping emissivity, this inference is conditional on the assumed ionizing photon production efficiency. 2. The halo-mass-only model prefers a positive halo-mass index, but this should not be read as evidence that massive halos leak ionizing photons more efficiently: it is the only way this model can reproduce the decline of f esc f_{\rm esc} with redshift, because low-mass halos increasingly dominate the halo population at early times, and the corresponding local slope is shallow ( d ​ ln ⁡ f esc / d ​ ln ⁡ M h ≈ 0.08 d\ln f_{\rm esc}/d\ln M_{\rm h}\approx 0.08 at 10 10 ​ M ⊙ 10^{10}\,M_{\odot} ). When redshift and halo mass are varied simultaneously, the halo-mass index is consistent with zero, and the data attribute the evolution of the global escape fraction to redshift rather than to halo mass. An escape fraction that decreases steeply with halo mass, as found in simulations of feedback-regulated low-mass galaxies [ 107 , 86 , 109 ] , is disfavored, although a mild decrease is not excluded (see Figure 1 ). 3. All three variable models predict a nearly identical evolution of the global EoR observables, with reionization ending at z ≈ 6 z\approx 6 . The constant- f esc f_{\rm esc} model produces a higher ionizing emissivity at early times but converges to the same completion redshift and a very similar optical depth (see Figures 4 – 6 ). 4. At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology produced by SimFast21 is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the models reach a given stage of reionization within Δ ​ z ≲ 0.4 \Delta z\lesssim 0.4 of one another (see Figure 7 ). 5. The 21 cm power spectra agree to within ≈ 10 % \approx 10\% at matched stages, compared with a ≲ 1 % \lesssim 1\% residual from the matching procedure, and the f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) model remains closest to the constant reference, with median deviations below 2 % 2\% (see Figure 8 and Table 3 ). This level of agreement is consistent with that found by S. Hassan et al. [52] when replacing simple source models with sources from the Simba simulation. 6. Once calibrated against the same EoR and UVLF observations, the escape-fraction prescriptions are therefore strongly, though not perfectly, degenerate in both the globally averaged observables and the spatial statistics of the 21 cm field. Although f esc f_{\rm esc} is set by small-scale physics in the interstellar medium, these large-scale observables are sensitive mainly to its population-averaged value, which the calibration fixes to nearly the same evolution in all prescriptions, and only weakly to how f esc f_{\rm esc} is distributed among the halos resolved here. These observables alone therefore cannot distinguish a constant from a variable escape fraction, nor determine whether the evolution of f esc f_{\rm esc} is driven by halo mass or by redshift. Several extensions would sharpen these conclusions. Simulations at higher resolution, resolving the low-mass halos in which other studies find the strongest dependence of f esc f_{\rm esc} on halo mass, would test whether the degeneracy persists when these sources are included. Statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as the bubble size distribution, the bispectrum, and morphological measures, may be more sensitive to differences in ionization topology [ 58 , 1 ] , as may sightline statistics such as opacity fluctuations in the Ly α \alpha forest [ 66 ] and the 21 cm forest toward radio-loud sources [ 41 ] . Because 21 cm experiments measure the signal at fixed redshift rather than fixed neutral fraction, forecasts for SKA-Low that include the timing differences between models are needed to assess observability [ 5 ] . Finally, linking f esc f_{\rm esc} to observable galaxy properties, for example through the empirical relation with the UV continuum slope β \beta [ 20 ] , with its coefficients treated as free parameters, or freeing the ionizing photon production efficiency, would help break the degeneracy between f esc f_{\rm esc} and ξ ion \xi_{\rm ion} that limits the interpretation of the absolute escape fractions. Astropy [ 3 ] , Colossus [ 28 ] , CoReCon [ 43 ] , emcee [ 40 ] , Matplotlib [ 57 ] , Numpy [ 50 ] , SciPy [ 103 ] , Pulkit Sheoran Affiliation: School of Physical Sciences, Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Kolkata-700032, India Email: [ Email: ug23ps2957@iacs.res.in Ankita Bera Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA Email: [ Sultan Hassan Affiliation: Space Telescope Science Institute, 3700 San Martin Dr, Baltimore, MD 21218 Email: shassan@stsci.edu Abstract The escape fraction of ionizing photons, f esc f_{\rm esc} , is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) , and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) , against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow f esc f_{\rm esc} to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant- f esc f_{\rm esc} model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from ≈ 0.8 \approx 0.8 at z = 5 z=5 to ≈ 0.35 \approx 0.35 at z = 15 z=15 . The halo-mass-only model prefers f esc f_{\rm esc} increasing with halo mass, but this trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent f esc f_{\rm esc} . At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within ≈ 10 % \approx 10\% . These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the f esc f_{\rm esc} prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Ly α \alpha and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing. Keywords: Reionization — High-redshift galaxies — Intergalactic medium — Bayesian statistics show] pulkitsheoran022@gmail.com show] ankitabm@umd.edu I Introduction The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) marks the last major phase transition of the universe from a neutral to an ionized state [ 106 , 21 , for recent reviews, see] . The first stars and galaxies, which formed during the Cosmic Dawn, produced copious Lyman continuum (LyC) photons that ionized the neutral hydrogen in the surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM), forming ionized bubbles around them [ 4 , 112 , 26 ] . Over time, these bubbles grew and eventually overlapped, marking the completion of reionization. However, most of these ionizing photons could not escape their host galaxies and were instead absorbed by neutral gas and dust in the interstellar medium and circumgalactic medium [ 101 ] . The fraction that does escape into the IGM is referred to as the ionizing photon escape fraction ( f esc f_{\rm esc} ) [ 98 , 108 ] . Understanding f esc f_{\rm esc} is critical for establishing both the physical mechanisms and the timeline of reionization. Together with the ionizing photon production efficiency ( ξ ion \xi_{\rm ion} ) and the star formation history, it sets the ionizing emissivity, and therefore governs whether reionization proceeded rapidly or gradually and which sources drove it. Pre-JWST models combined with Planck observations suggest that star-forming galaxies produce enough ionizing photons to reionize the universe by z ∼ 6 z\sim 6 . S. L. Finkelstein et al. [35] , for example, argued that a low, halo-mass-dependent escape fraction with a global average of only a few percent ( ⟨ f esc ⟩ ≤ 5 % \langle f_{\rm esc}\rangle\leq 5\% ) is sufficient to complete reionization. That conclusion relies on several key assumptions, including star formation extending down to ultra-faint galaxies (a faint-end truncation at M UV ∼ − 13 M_{\rm UV}\sim-13 with photo-suppression quenching star formation below log ⁡ ( M h / M ⊙ ) ∼ 9 \log(M_{\rm h}/M_{\odot})\sim 9 in already-ionized regions), an ionizing photon production efficiency that rises modestly toward fainter, higher-redshift dwarfs ( log ⁡ ξ ion ∼ 25.2 \log\xi_{\rm ion}\sim 25.2 – 25.3 25.3 ), and a significant but subdominant active galactic nucleus (AGN) contribution at z ≲ 7 z\lesssim 7 . However, the JWST observations have revealed an overabundance of UV-luminous galaxies at z ≳ 9 z\gtrsim 9 [ 19 , 48 , 36 ] together with elevated ionizing efficiencies ( log ⁡ ξ ion ≈ 25.5 \log\xi_{\rm ion}\approx 25.5 – 26.0 26.0 ) [ 32 , 82 ] , which imply far more ionizing photons at early times. Taken at face value, these photons would complete reionization too early, in tension with the low CMB Thomson optical depth measured by Planck Collaboration et al. [90] and with Lyman- α \alpha forest measurements, which place the end of reionization near z ∼ 5.5 z\sim 5.5 [ 7 , 13 ] , later than the z ∼ 6 z\sim 6 endpoint assumed in earlier models, termed as “photon budget crisis” [ 82 ] . Several resolutions have been proposed, including bursty star formation inflating the observed UV luminosity function [ 99 ] , a shorter ionizing mean free path [ 8 ] , a truncation of the faint-end galaxy population [ 82 ] , and a revised ξ ion \xi_{\rm ion} [ 96 ] . The possibility we examine here is that the escape fraction of these abundant early galaxies is lower, and/or suppressed toward higher redshift, than low-redshift LyC leaker calibrations imply [ 39 ] . The IGM is opaque to the ionizing photons at high redshifts, so f esc f_{\rm esc} cannot be measured directly during this era [ 59 ] . We therefore rely on models that predict its behavior by constraining it against other available observables [ 92 , 81 , e.g.,] . Physically, f esc f_{\rm esc} is set by the interstellar medium (ISM) on scales far below those resolved in reionization simulations. Young stars emit most of their ionizing photons within the first few Myr, while still embedded in dense birth clouds that absorb them [ 62 , 69 ] . Photons escape mainly through low-column-density channels cleared by stellar and supernova feedback, so f esc f_{\rm esc} peaks only after a delay and varies strongly with the recent star formation history [ 62 , 69 ] . Processes that extend the ionizing output beyond this delay, such as binary stellar evolution [ 68 ] and runaway massive stars [ 62 ] , increase the escape fraction, although in the FIRE-2 simulations binaries raise ⟨ f esc ⟩ \langle f_{\rm esc}\rangle by only ≈ 25 \approx 25 –35% [ 70 ] . C. Howard et al. [56] suggest that the escape fraction is a strongly fluctuating quantity that depends on the mass of the star cluster and the turbulent structure of the gas cloud. M. Trebitsch et al. [101] , using a series of high-resolution radiation hydrodynamical simulations, find that f esc f_{\rm esc} in high-redshift galaxies can vary by several orders of magnitude over short timescales, driven primarily by supernova explosions that disrupt dense star-forming clumps and clear low-column-density channels through the halo. Averaged over a galaxy population, the escape fraction depends on the physical properties of the host galaxies [ 62 ] , which correlate with halo mass ( M h M_{\rm h} ) [ 109 ] . Simulations of the first galaxies find that feedback clears escape channels more easily in low-mass halos, giving an escape fraction that decreases with halo mass [ 107 , 86 , 109 , 63 ] , a trend adopted in several reionization models [ 87 , 35 ] . Because low-mass halos dominate at early times, such models imply a population-averaged escape fraction that increases with redshift, as also assumed in earlier emissivity models [ 47 , 65 ] . However, simulations disagree on the strength and even the sign of the resulting f esc f_{\rm esc} – M h M_{\rm h} trend [ 70 ] . We therefore treat any f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) relation as a population-averaged parametrization rather than a description of individual galaxies. While many models adopt a constant f esc f_{\rm esc} for convenience, this fails to capture the dynamics of galaxy evolution. For example, S. Mitra & A. Chatterjee [80] use a data-driven reionization model with a Gaussian Process Regression method to infer a redshift-dependent escape fraction, though that reconstruction relies on pre-JWST data. To capture the dynamics of the escape fraction, in this paper we consider three simple prescriptions of photon escape fraction that depend on redshift, halo mass, and the both: f esc ​ ( z ) f_{\rm esc}(z) , f esc ​ ( M h ) f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h}) and f esc ​ ( z , M h ) f_{\rm esc}(z,M_{\rm h}) , and compare with a constant f esc f_{\rm esc} baseline model of A. Bera et al. [10] . We constrain these models against JWST and EoR observables, namely the UV luminosity functions, the IGM neutral fraction, and the CMB optical depth, using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework to obtain posterior constraints on the model parameters and to trace the evolution of the escape fraction with redshift and/or halo mass. We then integrate our MCMC-calibrated f esc f_{\rm esc} prescriptions directly into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 [ 93 ] . While full radiative transfer codes such as C 2 -Ray [ 77 ] are more physically robust, they are computationally expensive. Other semi-numerical alternatives include excursion-set frameworks [ 79 , e.g., 21cmFAST ;] , one-dimensional radiative transfer schemes [ 44 , GRIZZLY ;] , explicitly photon-conserving algorithms [ 22 , 23 , SCRIPT ;] , abundance-matching approaches [ 100 , AMBER ;] , and models coupled to semi-analytic galaxy formation [ 58 , ASTRAEUS ;] . SimFast21 is based on the excursion-set formalism but populates the non-linear density field with resolved halos. This allows us to move beyond globally averaged reionization histories to the full three-dimensional ionization field, quantifying whether, and to what extent, an evolving escape fraction alters the morphology of ionized bubbles and the resulting 21-cm power spectra at fixed neutral fraction. This paper is organized as follows. In Section II , we describe the source model, combining the intrinsic ionizing photon production rate with our three f esc f_{\rm esc} parameterizations. Section III describes how the UV luminosity function, ionizing emissivity, neutral hydrogen fraction, and Thomson optical depth are computed in the model, and lists the observational data used to constrain them. In Section IV , we present the MCMC framework and our implementation of the f esc f_{\rm esc} models in SimFast21 . Section V presents the MCMC constraints on the escape fraction, followed by the ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra from the simulations. We summarize our conclusions and discuss future directions in Section VI . II Source model In this section we describe the source model that governs the ionizing photon budget, combining a prescription for the intrinsic photon production rate with the redshift- and halo-mass-dependent escape-fraction models. II.1 Ionization Rate, R ion R_{\rm ion} To quantify the intrinsic production rate of ionizing photons, we adopt the source model of S. Hassan et al. [51] , with the ionization rate, R ion R_{\rm ion} (in units of photons s -1 ) as a function of halo mass ( M h M_{\rm h} ) and redshift ( z z ), derived from radiative-transfer simulations [ 38 ] . This model has previously been calibrated against EoR observables [ 11 ] and JWST constraints [ 10 ] . II.2 The ionizing photon escape fraction The physical dependences of the population-averaged escape fraction remain uncertain, and previous studies have parameterized it as a function of either halo mass or redshift. We consider power-law parameterizations in both, following J. Park et al. [87] , who model f esc f_{\rm esc} as a power law in halo mass, and C.-A. A redshift-dependent escape fraction has been inferred from data-driven reionization models [ 80 ] and adopted in models of the UV background [ 47 , 34 ] . III Observational Constraints To constrain the free parameters of our f esc f_{\rm esc} models, we compare the model predictions against JWST and EoR observables.
